title: Debit call spread vs credit put spread: same payoff, different prices
summary: A debit call spread and a credit put spread at the same strikes have the same payoff in theory, but prices can differ. In the SoFi example, the 30/25 credit put spread paid $350, yet because of skew the call spread was the better deal. Before you trade, compare both versions across the strikes.

steps.caption: SoFi trades between the two strikes, 25 and 30.
A: buy the 25 call, sell the 30 call. You pay a debit.
B: sell the 30 put, buy the 25 put. You receive about $350 per spread.
In theory the two payoffs match. With skew, the call spread cost less, so it was the better trade.
Both break even at the same price. The cheaper side gives more reward for the same risk.

takeaways: A debit call spread and a credit put spread at the same strikes have the same theoretical payoff.
Skew can make one version cheaper than the other.
Check both versions across strikes and trade the one with better economics.
caveats: The speaker says this is education, not a trade recommendation; prices in the clip are partly cut off.
The model uses one IV for all legs, so it shows the theory, not the skew gap. Waitlist mention is promotional.
